proof:
Let $\beta$ be the largest actual depth. For upper semicontinuity, if $Y_j\to Y$ and $H$ is any closed halfspace containing $Y$, parallel enlargements of $H$ by a positive amount contain $Y_j$ eventually. Their finite masses decrease to $\mu(H)$ as the enlargement decreases to zero. Infimizing over $H$ gives the upper semicontinuity. The center of an interior ball in a positive fiber has positive depth because any containing ambient halfspace captures at least half that ball, including constant traces. Hence compactness of $S$ gives $\beta>0$ and a nonempty compact $\mathcal Y$.

A point $(p,y)$ outside the ordinary interior of its own fiber, with $y\in K_p$, admits a continuous unit supporting normal $u$ with $u\cdot y=h_{K_p}(u)$. Apply 155691fc3768c06f to the finite family of all nonempty integer fibers. They are compact convex and the required anchored Minkowski inclusion is furnished by convexity of $C$, even for lower-dimensional fibers. Its affine support slope $A$ makes the closed cap
$$
u\cdot x-A\cdot(z-p)\ge h_{K_p}(u)
$$
contain $(p,y)$ and restrict on every fiber to a subset of a hyperplane of zero $d$-volume. Thus every point in $\mathcal Y$ is own-interior.

Continuity of the own-fiber retained mass follows from 669858b8fc253d7c for each fixed positive body. There are finitely many bases, so $\tau$ is attained on $\mathcal Y$, and it is positive by the feasible indicator of a centered small ball. Any closed halfspace containing a positive convex combination of marks contains at least one input. Thus a combination of deepest marks remains deepest whenever its base is integral, because convexity of $C$ makes the target an actual sampled point. In particular the deepest marks in each fiber form a convex set. Fixed-body strict quasiconcavity of the retained mass gives at most one maximizer over such a set.

In an integral-target combination of marks in $\mathcal Y_\tau$, joint retained-cap concavity gives target retained mass at least $\tau$. It equals $\tau$ by maximality on $\mathcal Y$. The joint equality theorem now makes the input caps centered at their marks homothetic, with target the Minkowski combination. All input masses equal $\tau$, so the centered caps agree, including the target. For every integer base in the convex hull of the selected bases, a convex representation by them has such a target after omitting zero weights. Two bases of the same coordinate parity have an integral midpoint, so their caps are translates. This proves both base assertions.

The stratum $\mathcal Y_\tau$ is nonempty and finite, so energy attains a common positive maximum on $\mathcal Z$. A positive convex combination of $\mathcal Z$ with integral base is in $\mathcal Y_\tau$ by the preceding argument. All its input and target marks are own-interior and the target fiber contains the weighted Minkowski sum. The containing-body part of 5aeb5916857f97a9 gives target energy root at least the common selected root; maximality makes this equality. The same theorem gives exact target inclusion equality and positive homothety of the centered whole bodies. Changing variables in the energy integral scales it by the $d$th power of the homothety factor. Equal positive energies therefore force all factors to be one. The target lies in $\mathcal Z$ and the same-parity midpoint argument gives the bound on translation classes.

statement:
Let $n\ge0$, $d\ge1$, and let $C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d$ be a compact convex body whose integer fibers $K_p=\{x:(p,x)\in C\}$ have positive total $d$-volume. Include every nonempty integer fiber in the mixed set $S$ and let $\mu$ sum ordinary $d$-volume over these fibers. For $Y\in S$ define $\Delta(Y)=\inf_{H\ni Y}\mu(H)$ over all closed ambient halfspaces, and write $\mathcal Y$ for the points maximizing this depth. All points in $\mathcal Y$ are in the ordinary interiors of their own fibers. Use the physical retained mass $T_K(y)$ and its unique optimal cap $D_K(y)$, defined by maximizing $\int_K f$ over measurable $0\le f\le1$ with $\int_K(x-y)f(x)\,dx=0$.

There is an attained positive maximum $\tau$ of $T_{K_p}(y)$ over $(p,y)\in\mathcal Y$. Its attaining stratum $\mathcal Y_\tau$ has at most one mark at each base. For any positive convex combination of marks $(p_i,y_i)$ in this stratum whose target base $p=\sum_i\lambda_i p_i$ is integral, the target $(p,y)$ with $y=\sum_i\lambda_i y_i$ lies in $\mathcal Y_\tau$, and
$$
D_{K_{p_i}}(y_i)-y_i=D_{K_p}(y)-y\quad\text{for every }i,
\qquad D_{K_p}(y)=\sum_i\lambda_iD_{K_{p_i}}(y_i).
$$
The set of its bases equals the integer points of its convex hull, and at most $2^n$ translation classes of retained caps occur.

On $\mathcal Y_\tau$, let $\mathcal Z$ be the marks maximizing the ordinary projective energy
$$
E_K(y)=\inf_{a:\ 1+a\cdot(x-y)>0\ (x\in K)}\int_K[1+a\cdot(x-y)]^{-d-1}\,dx.
$$
Then $\mathcal Z$ is nonempty and finite. For each positive convex combination of its marks with integral target base, the target is in $\mathcal Z$ and
$$
K_{p_i}-y_i=K_p-y\quad\text{for every }i,
\qquad K_p=\sum_i\lambda_iK_{p_i}.
$$
There are at most $2^n$ translation classes of these centered whole fibers.
title: Physical retained-cap and energy strata on actual deepest points
